shared_turn_1.user_message: What happens to the DNA in blood transfusions? Why doesn’t it change your body when you have someone else’s DNA inside of you?
shared_turn_1.assistant_response:
Blood contains cells with DNA—mainly white blood cells and platelets; red blood cells lack nuclei. After transfusion, those donor cells function briefly, then age and are removed by your spleen/liver/immune system. Their DNA is broken down by enzymes and recycled.

It doesn’t change you because DNA only affects a cell if it’s inside a nucleus and expressed; it doesn’t jump into your own cells or integrate into your genome. So you may temporarily have a tiny amount of donor DNA, but it’s cleared and has no lasting effect.

The DNA is real, but transient, compartmentalized, and inert to your genome.
